title: Berdyaev and Shestov
keyWorks: L. Shestov, The Apotheosis of Groundlessness (All Things Are Possible) (1905)
N. Berdyaev, The Meaning of the Creative Act (1916)
N. Berdyaev, The Destiny of Man (1931)
N. Berdyaev, Self-Knowledge (Dream and Reality) (1949, posthumous)
summary: Nikolai Berdyaev (1874–1948) and Lev Shestov (1866–1938) were Russian philosophers and longtime friends who both ended up as émigrés in France. Berdyaev built a philosophy of freedom and creativity: a human being, he was convinced, is called not only to obey but to create something new. Shestov spent his life rebelling against the rule of "necessity" and of general truths that cannot hear the living, suffering person. Both were religious thinkers; their views are presented here as their own search, not as a doctrine you are asked to accept.
onEmotions: For both of them, feelings are not an obstacle to reason but the voice of a living person, which general explanations must not drown out. Berdyaev drew fine distinctions between fear and dread, between longing and boredom, and showed how fear, malice or habit can enslave a person, while freedom and creativity bring them back to themselves. The main danger, he believed, was "objectification": a living person turned into a thing, a role or a function, including in their own eyes. Shestov defended the suffering person's right to cry out, to protest and to disagree: he argued with any philosophy that teaches resignation to the inevitable, and saw in reason's "self-evident truths" not a consolation but a prison. Together they invite you to take your feelings seriously, as the truth of a person rather than a mistake to be corrected as quickly as possible.

anxiety.text: Anxiety tells you there is no solid ground under your feet, and that is frightening. Lev Shestov called one of his books The Apotheosis of Groundlessness: rather than soothing anxiety by sliding a ready-made system underneath it, he doubted that such firm ground exists at all. For centuries, Shestov thought, philosophers have built systems to calm us down, but these constructions often just block our view of living life; we have to learn to live without guarantees. Berdyaev would add that uncertainty is the other side of freedom: where everything is settled in advance there is no anxiety, but there is no creativity either. From their point of view, anxiety is not a malfunction but the price of an open future. You don't have to defeat it; you can carefully bear it, the way you bear each step on an unfamiliar road.
anxiety.practice: Write down: "I don't know how things will go with…" and let that not-knowing simply stay on the page for a while, without turning it straight into a plan.

fear.text: Fear is a strong and honest feeling, and Berdyaev took it seriously. In The Destiny of Man he distinguished fear, which faces a concrete danger in this world, from dread, which faces the abyss, the deepest mysteries of existence. Fear, for Berdyaev, is one of the main forces that make a person a slave: out of fear we submit, we hide, we give up our own freedom. But he did not call on anyone to "stop being afraid" by sheer willpower. He believed that inner freedom and a creative attitude to life gradually loosen fear's grip. Seen this way, your fear is no disgrace. But it is worth asking: what is it trying to make me submit to right now, and is there a step, however small, that is truly mine?
fear.practice: Ask yourself: "If fear weren't deciding for me, what small step would I take?" Write it down; you don't have to take it right now.

sadness.text: Sadness doesn't always need comforting; sometimes it needs to be heard. Lev Shestov spent his life arguing with philosophers who rush to explain suffering with general truths: "that's how the world works," "it is reasonable and necessary." In his books the voice of the suffering person, the biblical Job or Dostoevsky's underground man, matters more than any orderly system. Shestov believed sorrow has a truth of its own that reason has no right to cancel. Berdyaev wrote about toska, a longing that reaches toward something greater than everyday life. From their point of view, your sadness may not be a mistake that needs urgent fixing but a sign that you sense the depth of life and refuse to accept flat explanations.
sadness.practice: Write a few lines about your sadness without explaining it or consoling yourself; just give it a voice.

grief.text: Grief does not accept comforts like "it was meant to happen." And Lev Shestov would be on your side here. The main adversary in his philosophy is "necessity": the conviction that whatever has happened is reasonable and could not have been otherwise. In Athens and Jerusalem he argues with the whole tradition that teaches humble acceptance of the irreparable, and recalls the idea of the medieval theologian Peter Damian that nothing is impossible for God. For Shestov, a religious thinker, this was a hope beyond the reach of logic. You don't have to share his faith to hear his lesson: your protest against the loss is not immaturity but the voice of a love that will not consent. Grief may be allowed to disagree.
grief.practice: Write a few sentences about what in this loss you do not agree with. You don't have to be resigned on paper.

loneliness.text: Berdyaev knew loneliness from childhood: in Self-Knowledge he admits that all his life he felt a certain estrangement from the world around him. He even devoted a book to the subject, Solitude and Society (in Russian, I and the World of Objects: An Essay in the Philosophy of Solitude and Communion). His idea is that loneliness is sharpest among people, when relationships turn into functions, roles and exchange, into what he called "objectification." That kind of sociability does not cure loneliness. What cures it is communion: the meeting of one person with another, of "I" with "Thou," where neither becomes an object for the other. So loneliness, for Berdyaev, says nothing about your inadequacy; it speaks of a person's longing for a real meeting. That is found not in the number of contacts but in a single genuine one.
loneliness.practice: Remember someone with whom you once had a real meeting: not a role, but a conversation. Write them a couple of words, or simply recall that conversation in detail.

anger.text: Anger is the energy of disagreement, and Russian existential thought treated rebellion with respect. Shestov rose up against "self-evident truths," the things everyone accepts as inevitable; the hero of Dostoevsky's Notes from Underground, whom he valued so highly, refuses to accept even "twice two makes four" if it crushes a living person. Berdyaev, too, saw protest as an expression of freedom. But he also warned that malice and hatred easily make a person a slave of the very one they are fighting. A rebellion that merely repeats violence does not set anyone free. From their point of view, anger deserves to be acknowledged: it tells you that you disagree with something. Then ask yourself: how can I keep the strength of my disagreement without letting anger enslave me?
anger.practice: Write down: "I don't agree that…" Then: "My free disagreement could take the form of…"

shame.text: Shame arises when we see ourselves through someone else's eyes, eyes that assess and condemn. Berdyaev would call this the gaze of the world of "objectification": there a person becomes an object, a set of qualities, functions and social ratings. But for Berdyaev a person can never be reduced to how they look from the outside. The person is a mystery; not a part of some whole, not an item on someone else's list. What matters most is the inner, free, creative core, which no outside judgment can exhaust or cancel. Shame, from this point of view, shows that you have fallen under a gaze that turns you into a thing. You can acknowledge that gaze, and remember that you are more than what can be seen of you right now.
shame.practice: Finish the sentence: "Right now I'm seen as…, but there is also … in me," even if only with one word.

guilt.text: Guilt is heavy, and Berdyaev thought carefully about how to live with it. In The Destiny of Man he described three kinds of ethics. The ethics of law judges actions by rules and easily turns into endless condemnation. The ethics of redemption, which grew out of Christianity, speaks of mercy and the possibility of forgiveness. The ethics of creativity sees a human being as someone able to create something new and so to answer the past with more than repentance. Berdyaev criticized the ethics of law because it can crush a person under the weight of guilt. From this point of view, guilt is a legitimate signal but not a final verdict. It can become not self-punishment but a creative response: what new thing can I do now?
guilt.practice: Ask yourself: "What small new action could be my answer to what I feel guilty about?" Write it down.

envy.text: Envy compares, and comparison, for Berdyaev, is always a little untrue to a person. He insisted that each person is unique and incomparable: you cannot line them up with others and measure them by a common yardstick. Comparison is only possible in the world of "objectification," where people become carriers of qualities, statuses and achievements, and there someone is always "higher." But creativity, which Berdyaev considered every person's calling, does not compete: each creates their own, and no one's gift takes another's place. Envy, from this point of view, is a sign that you are looking at yourself as an object in a common queue. It can be turned into a question: what touched me in someone else's life, and what gift of my own does that point to?
envy.practice: Instead of "they have it and I don't," write: "What moves me in their life is… so what matters to me is…"

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy are when nothing inside responds. Berdyaev knew these states and described them honestly. He believed that the world we usually live in, the world of "objectification," where everything has become objects, functions and duties, gives no meaning by itself: meaning, he was convinced, is born from a person's freedom and creativity. When the creative fire goes out, the world looks flat and grey. But emptiness, in his view, is not proof that there is no meaning; it is the experience of meaning's absence, and that experience itself speaks of a thirst for meaning. Berdyaev believed a human being can bring something new into the world. Even a tiny creative gesture is a first movement out of emptiness, not a duty to conquer it.
emptiness.practice: Do one small thing your own way, with no use and no judgment: draw a line, move an object, write a single sentence.

confusion.text: Confusion is when the old answers have stopped working. Lev Shestov thought this state is closer to the truth than it seems. All his life he argued with philosophical systems that promise to explain everything. In his view, real thinking begins where "self-evident truths" collapse, the things we had taken as beyond doubt. He often wrote his books in aphorisms and fragments rather than building them into a system: life, he believed, does not fit into a tidy order. From this point of view, confusion is not a sign of stupidity or weakness but a moment when you see the world without the ready-made scenery. Answers will come, but perhaps this time they will be your own answers rather than borrowed ones.
confusion.practice: Write down one "self-evident" thing you have started to doubt, and ask: where did I get the idea that it's so in the first place?

fatigue.text: Tiredness and burnout are a legitimate response, and Berdyaev can help you see them more deeply. In Slavery and Freedom he described many forms of slavery: to the state, to money, to public opinion, to one's own ideas about oneself. One of the least noticeable is when a person dissolves into functions and duties and becomes merely someone playing a role. Berdyaev called this "objectification": a living person turned into a mechanism. Such a life is draining even when there isn't all that much to do, because it leaves no room for freedom and creativity. From this point of view, burnout is not laziness but the resistance of a person who refuses to be nothing but a function. That tiredness deserves to be heard as a request for freedom.
fatigue.practice: Ask yourself: "In which of my roles am I least myself right now?" Just notice it, without changing anything yet.

boredom.text: Boredom seems trivial, but Berdyaev took it seriously. He distinguished toska, longing, from boredom. Longing, in his thinking, points upward: it is a yearning for something greater, for meaning, for another world, and there is movement in it. Boredom is when there is no movement: the world seems flat, finite, repetitive, as if there were nothing in it to wait for. From this point of view, boredom is not simply a lack of entertainment, and new entertainment does not cure it. You can try to turn it into longing, that is, to give it a direction. It's enough to ask yourself: what am I actually missing, what do I lack right now? Sometimes a very alive desire hides behind boredom.
boredom.practice: Finish the sentence: "I'm bored because I'm missing…" and notice what boredom turns into once it has a direction.

joy.text: Joy can be accepted without reservations, and Berdyaev knew how to value it. He wrote about creative uplift, the state in which a person feels free and able to create something new. Joy, in his view, is a sign that at that moment the person is living from their freedom rather than from compulsion. Shestov, for all his focus on tragedy, also argued against the idea that reason has the right to take life's living gifts away in the name of "necessity" and "order." From their point of view, joy doesn't need to be justified, earned, or clouded by the thought that it will soon pass. It is a moment of real life in which you are more than a function or a duty. It's enough to notice it.
joy.practice: Pause and name what in this joy is truly yours: free, not set from outside.

love.text: Berdyaev saw love and tenderness as one of the ways a person comes out of loneliness. In The Destiny of Man he wrote that love is directed at a concrete, unrepeatable person, not at their qualities or usefulness. To love, as he understood it, is to see in another their true image, the idea of them that runs deeper than their flaws. For Berdyaev, a Christian thinker, this image had a religious meaning; but his thought makes sense without faith too: love sees more in a person than others do. Tenderness is the response to that fragile uniqueness. From this point of view, your feeling is not naivety but a special kind of sight worth protecting.
love.practice: Think of someone you love and name one trait that you see in them, and perhaps few others do.

gratitude.text: Gratitude is the feeling that something has been given to you not by right or by law but as something extra. From Shestov's point of view, one could say it is one of those experiences reason cannot fully explain. Reason looks for necessity: everything must be earned, derived, justified. Gratitude lives where something happens that no one was obliged to give. Shestov, a religious thinker, linked such a space with faith, for which "all things are possible," as opposed to the "Athens" of reason. Berdyaev would add that real gratitude is not servile: it is not a debt but a free response of the person. You can simply let yourself notice that some things in your life have been gifts.
gratitude.practice: Recall one thing you were given even though no one had to give it. Write down who or what it was.

hope.text: Hope, from Shestov's point of view, is a revolt against the verdict "it cannot be otherwise." His main adversary is necessity: the conviction that the laws of reason and nature settle once and for all what is possible and what is not. In Athens and Jerusalem he set "Athens," the world of reason and inevitable truths, against "Jerusalem," biblical faith, for which, he was convinced, nothing is impossible. You don't have to share his faith; his thought matters without it: what seems inevitable today is not always the last word about the world. Berdyaev echoed him in his own way: freedom means the future is not decided in advance. Hope, in this light, is not naivety but faithfulness to the openness of life.
hope.practice: Name one "it cannot be otherwise" belief that holds you right now. Ask yourself: is this really a law, or only a habit of thinking?

nostalgia.text: Berdyaev knew nostalgia firsthand: expelled from Russia in 1922, he spent the rest of his life in emigration, and near the end wrote a philosophical autobiography, Self-Knowledge. In it he observes that remembering is never a passive, exact reconstruction of the past: as we remember, we select, illuminate, transform. Berdyaev distinguished the time that carries things away and destroys them from an inner, "existential" time in which what we have lived through keeps its depth. From this point of view, nostalgia is not only a flight backward but also the creative work of memory: you are not simply losing the past, you keep giving it meaning. Whatever was genuine in it remains part of you.
nostalgia.practice: Choose one memory you miss and write down what in it was most real for you, the thing you want to keep.

craving.text: A craving is a sharp "I want it right now," and there is nothing shameful in it: that is how strong urges work. Berdyaev, the philosopher of freedom, would say that at this moment two forces are arguing inside you. One is the urge, which demands things immediately and repeats the familiar loop. The other is the freedom of the person, which is able to pause. Slavery and Freedom has a chapter on "man's slavery to himself": Berdyaev showed that we can be enslaved not only by outside things but by what is our own. And he stressed that freedom is not given once and for all; it is carried out again and again. If yesterday went differently, today this freedom is still yours. A wave of craving rises and falls; every wave you wait out is a small act of freedom, not a feat of willpower.
craving.practice: When the craving comes, set a timer for ten minutes and simply watch it like the weather: where it sits in your body, whether it's growing or fading. Then decide afresh.

addiction.text: Addiction is a long loop, and Berdyaev would be the last to call it a moral failure. He sharply criticized the "ethics of law," which only hands down verdicts, and believed a human being is greater than any of their falls. A person, for Berdyaev, never fully coincides with what happens to them: a core of freedom remains, even when life has been built around one single thing. Shestov would add a protest against a false "necessity": the thought "this is who I am, and it will never be different" is not a law of the universe but a verdict that can be contested. The way out of the loop is rarely walked alone: Berdyaev believed a person opens up in communion, in meeting others. Where you are understood without judgment, freedom returns more easily.
addiction.practice: Think about whether there is a person or a community nearby, a mutual-help group, for example, where you would be understood without judgment. Just name it for yourself; you don't need to decide anything.

hangover.text: The morning after: a heavy body, anxiety, shame, scraps of last night. In hours like these an inner court usually convenes: "how could you?" Berdyaev would call this voice the "ethics of law," a morality that only judges and punishes. He believed such morality does not free a person but crushes them, and he set against it an ethics of mercy that sees a person as greater than their act. Shestov, for his part, argued all his life against the idea that the past decides once and for all, mercilessly, who we are. From their point of view, what matters now is not to pass sentence on yourself but to look after yourself: give yourself calm and rest. Working out what happened, and talking to people if you need to, can come later, more calmly.
hangover.practice: Say one sentence to yourself not as a judge but as a merciful friend: "You're having a hard time right now; let's just rest first."

euphoria.text: A flash of euphoria feels as if every door were open. Berdyaev knew states of uplift well: he wrote about creative ecstasy, when a person seems to break through the limits of the everyday world, and he did not consider such moments false. But he also described the "tragedy of creativity": the impulse reaches for the infinite, yet it takes shape in finite, limited things, and after the peak a cooling inevitably follows. Knowing this doesn't spoil the high; it makes it more honest. You can enjoy the sense of possibility without demanding that it last forever, and without rushing to turn every flash into big decisions. Let the uplift be a hint about what you want; you can bring it to life later, once things are calmer.
euphoria.practice: Write down in a word or two what seems so possible right now. It's a note about your desires; come back to it in a few days.

crash.text: The drop after a high hits hard: a moment ago everything seemed possible, and now it's all grey. Berdyaev described a similar rhythm and called it the "tragedy of creativity." The creative impulse, he wrote, strives toward a new world and a new life, but in the end it takes shape in finite things, a book, an event, a result, and after the peak comes a cooling. For him this was not proof that the impulse had been a deception but a feature of the human condition: we strive toward the infinite while living in the finite. From this point of view, the drop does not cancel what happened at the peak, and it doesn't mean you are "broken." It is the same wave in a different phase; there's no need to hurry the next rise.
crash.practice: Name one thing that has stayed with you after the high, however small. It's real, even though the elation is gone.

panic.text: Panic is terrifying: a wave of dread washes over you, your heart pounds, your breathing goes ragged. A wave like this usually peaks and recedes within a few minutes. In his book on Kierkegaard, Shestov wrote about a dread that seizes a person and seems to paralyze their will; he did not regard it as weakness and saw in it one of the deepest human experiences. From Berdyaev's point of view one might add that freedom lives not in an abstract mind but in a living person, with a body and a breath. So in a moment of panic you don't need to decide, understand or conquer anything. It's enough to help your body ride out the wave, and let the dread be there without obeying it.
panic.practice: Put your feet flat on the floor, breathe out slowly, making the out-breath longer than the in-breath, and name five things you can see. Repeat until the wave starts to ebb.

dread.text: Existential dread, the "what's the point of it all," the abyss, finitude, is a very heavy experience, and Berdyaev considered it neither shameful nor a sickness. He distinguished fear of a concrete danger from the dread that arises when a person touches the ultimate questions of being. For Berdyaev, this dread is a sign of a person's depth, of the fact that they cannot be satisfied with a flat world. Shestov defended all his life the right to ask such questions and to refuse soothing answers. But neither saw dread as the last word: for Berdyaev the answer to the abyss was creativity and communion, bringing something new into the world and meeting others. You don't have to settle the question "what for" today; you can live with it without being left alone with it.
dread.practice: Write down your "what for" question exactly as it sounds inside you. Then add one thing that was alive for you today anyway: a person, a task, a moment.

fomo.text: The fear of missing out feels as if real life were happening somewhere else. Berdyaev would call this the pressure of the "world of objectification," of general standards by which life is judged from the outside. All his life he defended the person against dissolving into the general: into fashion, majority opinion, the standard of a "proper" life. A person, for Berdyaev, is unique, and their path cannot be compared with anyone else's, just as you can't compare two different poems by their number of lines. From this point of view, the only life you can miss is your own, not someone else's. The fear of missing out can become a useful question: what do I want, as opposed to the picture I've been shown?
fomo.practice: Ask yourself: "If no one would ever find out where I was or what I did, what would I want today?" Write down the first thing that comes.

sleepless.text: Lying awake with your thoughts at three in the morning is agonizing: the mind spins and there are no answers. Shestov would say that at night something happens to you that by day you are protected from by "self-evident truths," the familiar, reassuring ones. For a while they vanish, and the questions rise to their full height. Shestov respected such questions and did not consider them an illness. But he also showed that a reason trying to settle them for good often just goes round in circles: the ultimate questions have no answer that can be derived like a theorem. From this point of view, night thoughts don't demand an immediate solution, and you don't have to defeat them. You can admit that the question is real, and set it aside, the way you set a heavy book aside until morning.
sleepless.practice: Write the night's question on a slip of paper and add: "A real question. I'll come back to it in the daytime." Then shift your attention to a slow out-breath.

betrayal.text: Betrayal hurts so much because you trusted not a function but a person. Berdyaev can help you name what happened. In true communion, the meeting of one person with another, neither is a means for the other. Betrayal is the moment you were turned into an object: an obstacle, a resource, a bargaining chip. Hence the particular pain: your very person has been wounded. But Berdyaev also insisted on something else: a person cannot be destroyed by being treated like a thing. That you were not seen speaks of the other's limits, not of your worth. The pain has to be lived through. As for forgiveness, from the standpoint of his philosophy of freedom, if it comes at all, it can only be a free act, never an obligation.
betrayal.practice: Write: "I was treated like…, but I am…" Finish the second part the way you yourself know yourself.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is a mix of love, fear and pain, and it's hard not to feel it. From Berdyaev's point of view, one might say that in jealousy love runs into the temptation of possession. He believed genuine love is directed toward a free person, and freedom cannot be appropriated: another human being cannot belong to us like a thing. Berdyaev wrote a great deal about how people become slaves of what they own or want to own. In this perspective, jealousy is the fear that the beloved's freedom will turn into loss. That fear is understandable. But it also contains a recognition that love is precious precisely because it is free: it is given, not held onto. You can let jealousy have its say and ask what it is really asking for: reassurance, attention, a conversation.
jealousy.practice: Finish the sentence: "What my jealousy is really asking for is…" and consider whether you could ask for that directly.

resentment.text: An old grievance is a weight you carry for years, sometimes no longer remembering all the details. From Berdyaev's point of view, one might say that a grievance living inside you for a long time becomes one of the forms of slavery he wrote about: you end up tied to the person who hurt you and keep living in their shadow. At the same time, Berdyaev opposed any compulsion in spiritual life, and so also a forced "let it go and forgive." His answer lies rather in creativity: a life that builds something new gradually stops revolving around the wound. Shestov would add that no one has the right to demand that you agree with injustice. You can ask not "how do I forgive" but "what do I want to create in a life where this grievance is no longer the main thing."
resentment.practice: Write down one thing you'd like to create or do in the near future, something that has nothing to do with the grievance.

heartbreak.text: A broken heart is a pain that shouldn't be rushed. Shestov would side with your refusal to accept it: he believed philosophy too often teaches resignation, "these things happen, it's the law of life," and so drowns out the cry of a living person. His favorite example is Job, who rejects his friends' explanations and keeps arguing. Berdyaev, for his part, saw a tragic depth in love: it is directed at what is eternal in another person, yet lives in a fragile, finite world where meetings can end. From their point of view, your pain is not naivety or weakness but a measure of how real the love was. It doesn't need a quick explanation. You can allow yourself to grieve and to disagree.
heartbreak.practice: Write a few sentences in the first person, like Job: no explanations or conclusions, just how you are right now.

impostor.text: Impostor syndrome is the fear that any minute now it will come out that you are not who people take you for. Berdyaev would suggest looking at it differently. He distinguished the person from the social role. A role is a function in the world of "objectification," with its positions, ratings and expectations; a person is a living mystery that never fully coincides with any role. That's why anyone who looks at themselves honestly feels, in some sense, "not quite in their place": their inner life is larger and more complex than any job title. This is not deception but a sign that you are a person, not a function. Your doubt may mean not "I'm pretending" but "I'm more than how I'm seen from outside."
impostor.practice: Write two lines: "My role is…" and "And I am…" Fill in the second not with a job title but with what truly matters to you.

self_hatred.text: Self-hatred and the inner critic cause real pain, and you don't have to agree with that voice. Berdyaev would call it the voice of the "ethics of law," a morality that only judges, passes sentence and is never satisfied. He believed such an ethics can crush a person, and that it forgets the main thing: a person is not a sum of deeds and flaws but an unrepeatable image that runs deeper than any mistake. Shestov argued all his life with "general truths" that speak in everyone's name and cannot see the living person. The inner critic, too, speaks in general truths: "you always," "you never." But it doesn't know the whole of you. You are more than its verdict.
self_hatred.practice: Write out one of the critic's sentences that uses "always" or "never," and find at least one exception to it in your life.

helplessness.text: Helplessness, the feeling that nothing depends on you, is exhausting, and it's understandable. Shestov wrote a great deal about people in hopeless situations, about Job and the characters of Dostoevsky and Tolstoy, and never demanded that they "pull themselves together." He believed that even when a person is powerless to change something, they are not obliged to accept that powerlessness as the final truth about the world: refusing to agree with "necessity" is already an inner movement. Berdyaev would add that freedom is not only an outward possibility of action but an inner dimension of the person that circumstances cannot take away entirely. From this point of view, powerlessness in outward things does not mean powerlessness in everything. You keep the right to choose how you relate to what is happening.
helplessness.practice: Divide a sheet of paper into two halves: "what isn't in my power" and "how I can relate to it." Fill in the second with at least one line.

procrastination.text: "I can't get started" is a familiar torment. Berdyaev, the philosopher of creativity, would explain it like this: every beginning is a creative act, and creativity, he was convinced, brings into the world something that wasn't there before. Such a beginning always involves risk and freedom, so it's no wonder a person freezes in front of it. Berdyaev also wrote about the "tragedy of creativity": the idea is always bigger than its realization, and whatever comes out will inevitably be more modest than what you imagined. Perhaps you're holding back precisely because you sense that gap in advance. But the gap can't be removed, and it says nothing about your inability. You can allow yourself an imperfect beginning; humans never get any other kind.
procrastination.practice: Start with a "bad" draft: spend five minutes on a first step, having given it permission in advance to be imperfect.

uprooted.text: Both thinkers lived through being torn from home. In 1922 Berdyaev was expelled from Soviet Russia on the so-called "philosophers' ship," and afterwards lived near Paris. Shestov emigrated in the early 1920s and also settled in France. Remarkably, long before that, Shestov had titled a book The Apotheosis of Groundlessness. "Groundlessness" was for him not only a misfortune but also the honest position of a thinking person who doesn't lean on ready-made foundations. Losing your ground is painful, and it can be mourned. But, from their point of view, a person can live and think without firm ground underfoot, finding support in freedom, in friendship (they themselves were friends for decades), in their work.
uprooted.practice: Name one support you have regardless of place: a person, a task, a habit of thought. Write it down as your "portable ground."

overload.text: Overload from information noise is a legitimate tiredness, and Berdyaev would recognize something familiar in it. He wrote about the "world of objectification," where everything turns into the external: objects, facts, functions, streams. In such a world a person lives more and more outwardly and less and less inside themselves. An endless feed is an almost perfect picture of that world: a stream of objects in which the living person gets lost. Berdyaev believed the real life of a person comes from within, from freedom, reflection, creativity, communion. When there's too much of the outer, no room is left for the inner. From this point of view, overload is not your inability to "cope" but the resistance of a person asking to come back to themselves.
overload.practice: Put your phone down and ask yourself: "What am I thinking right now on my own, not from the feed?" Write down one thought of your own.

unreality.text: The feeling that nothing is quite real is unsettling and disorienting, and it deserves to be spoken of gently. Berdyaev has an idea that makes this experience feel less alien. He believed that the familiar world of "objectification," the world of objects, roles and functions, is not the deepest reality. Sometimes that familiar scenery suddenly looks like cardboard, and a person gets frightened. But Berdyaev knew where to look for what is truly real: in the living person, in freedom, in communion, the meeting of "I" and "Thou." For him the most real thing was not the abstract but the concrete: this person, this feeling, this conversation. From this point of view, when the world feels unreal, you can lean on what is closest and most alive: a voice, a touch, a meeting.
unreality.practice: Touch something warm or rough and describe the sensation in one word. Then text or call someone close to you.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare gift, and you want it to last. Berdyaev would call it a moment when a person breaks through the familiar world of objects toward something greater, toward what he called the world of spirit. For him, a religious thinker, such moments were connected with God; but the experience he describes is familiar to non-believers too: the sense that reality is deeper than it usually appears. What Shestov valued in life was precisely what doesn't fit reason's calculations: the unexpected, the improbable, the miraculous. From their point of view, your awe doesn't need to be explained or reduced to something simple. It is a window that opened for a moment. You can simply stand by it for a while.
awe.practice: Stay in this feeling for one more minute without naming it; just let it be.

relief.text: Relief feels like a hand that was gripping you has let go. Shestov would understand this feeling from the inside. His philosophy is a long argument with "necessity," with the conviction that bad things are inevitable and everything is settled in advance. Relief is a small refutation of that conviction: what you feared didn't happen, happened differently, or simply let go. In moments like these you can see that the world is not as closed as it seemed while you were anxious. Berdyaev would see in relief a moment of liberation: a person held in fear's grip breathes freely again. From their point of view, you don't need to hurry to replace relief with a new worry. It reminds you that the future is open, and that openness holds good things too.
relief.practice: Breathe out slowly and write: "I was afraid that…, but it turned out…"

calm.text: Calm and peacefulness are things you just want to live in. Berdyaev, for all his restless temperament, knew the value of inner quiet. He believed the real life of a person comes from within, from the depth of the spirit, not from the outer bustle of the world of objects. Calm, from this point of view, is not inaction but a moment when a person is enslaved neither by fear, nor by haste, nor by other people's expectations. It is one of the forms of freedom: nothing is ordering you around right now. In The Meaning of the Creative Act Berdyaev called the human being the point where two worlds intersect, the outer and the spiritual; in calm, the second becomes easier to hear. You don't need to do anything with this feeling; it's enough to stay in it.
calm.practice: Sit still for a minute and notice: what has no power over me right now? Just name it.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is one of Berdyaev's central themes. His book The Meaning of the Creative Act is subtitled An Essay in the Justification of Man, and in it he argues that a human being is called not only to obey laws and atone for guilt but to create. Creativity, for Berdyaev, continues the creation of the world, bringing into it what was not there before; for him, a Christian thinker, it was the human response to God's idea of that person. But even outside a religious context his thought is encouraging: your inspiration is not a whim but an expression of the deepest thing in you, your freedom. Berdyaev also knew the "tragedy of creativity": the realization is always more modest than the impulse. That's no reason to wait for perfection; it's a reason to begin.
inspiration.practice: Write down the first, rawest form of what inspires you, without improving it. Let the impulse leave a trace.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is one of those feelings that are embarrassing to admit even to yourself. Lev Shestov especially valued Dostoevsky for daring to show the "underground" movements of the soul, what people usually hide behind respectable words. In Dostoevsky and Nietzsche: The Philosophy of Tragedy, Shestov argued that the truth about a human being often begins exactly where the decent explanations end. From his point of view, one might say that honestly noticing schadenfreude in yourself is not a fall but a step toward a living truth about yourself. Berdyaev would add something else: a person is not reducible to individual movements of the soul; they are larger than those and free in how they respond to them. Schadenfreude can tell you about your tiredness, hurt or rivalry. But it doesn't define who you are or what you will do next.
schadenfreude.practice: Write honestly: "I felt relieved at someone else's failure because…" Don't justify or scold yourself; just finish the sentence.

contempt.text: Contempt arises when another person seems lower, smaller, less worthy. Nikolai Berdyaev wrote about "objectification," turning a living person into an object, a function, a label. For him this is one of the main forms of slavery, both for the one who is objectified and for the one who objectifies. From Berdyaev's point of view, one might say that contempt is exactly this kind of objectification: the other person becomes "that sort" for you, stupid, weak, empty, and stops being a mystery. Berdyaev insisted that every person is unique and cannot be reduced to their deeds or their social role. This doesn't mean approving of everything a person does; Berdyaev himself could be harsh in his judgments. But contempt closes the door, while recognizing the person leaves it ajar, above all for you yourself.
contempt.practice: Silently name one thing about this person that you don't know and can't know. Notice whether the contempt shifts.

disgust.text: Disgust, at people, at a situation, sometimes at yourself, can be sudden and strong. In his autobiography Self-Knowledge, Nikolai Berdyaev admitted that all his life he felt a sense of estrangement from the world: much of everyday life seemed heavy, oppressive, repellent to him. He wasn't ashamed of this feeling; he tried to understand it. In his view, the world of "objectification," of frozen forms, rules and conventions, really can repel a living person. Disgust is often directed not at people as such but at what has frozen in them, gone dead, become mechanical. Against this Berdyaev set freedom and creativity. From this point of view, one might say disgust is a signal of longing for what is alive. Instead of suppressing it, you can ask: what genuine, free, living thing am I missing right now?
disgust.practice: Write down what disgusts you. Then the opposite: "What's alive and real for me is…" Name one example.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is a natural response to pain that's been inflicted on you. Nikolai Berdyaev reflected on it in The Destiny of Man. He criticized the "ethics of law," in which justice comes down to retribution, and observed with unexpected bluntness that behind the wish to punish the guilty, "good" people often hide a thirst for revenge, an almost vindictive pleasure. Berdyaev believed retribution keeps a person enslaved to the evil done to them: you go on living by its rules. Against this he set the "ethics of creativity," in which a person answers evil not by repeating it but by creating something new. From his point of view, the wish for revenge is an understandable feeling you can acknowledge without shame. But you can act from freedom: protect yourself, name the injustice, without becoming what you are rising up against.
revenge.practice: Ask yourself: "If I answered not with revenge but with something new and free, what would it be?" Write down at least one idea.

anger_at_loved.text: Getting angry with the people closest to you, a partner, parents, children, and then feeling ashamed of it is very human. In Slavery and Freedom Nikolai Berdyaev wrote that a person can end up enslaved to the family and the roles it imposes: "the good son," "the patient mother," "the dependable partner." When a role presses too hard, the living person inside resists, and that resistance often breaks out as anger. From his point of view, one might say that anger at loved ones is often aimed not at the people themselves but at the tightness of the roles you have both ended up in. Berdyaev did not deny love within the family; he believed a real meeting is possible where people see each other as persons rather than functions. You can acknowledge the anger, and find a form for it that doesn't wound the people you love.
anger_at_loved.practice: Finish the sentence: "I'm not angry at you yourself but at having to be…" Name the role that's pressing on you right now.

ambivalence.text: Loving someone close to you and at the same time not being able to stand them is a contradiction that's hard to bear. Nikolai Berdyaev considered Dostoevsky the greatest expert on human contradictions. In Dostoevsky: An Interpretation (Dostoevsky's Worldview) he wrote that Dostoevsky showed the human being as polar, torn by opposing forces: in his characters love can be intertwined with hatred, tenderness with tormenting. Berdyaev saw nothing monstrous in this; for him it was a sign of the depth and freedom of human nature. A person is not a machine that runs in one direction. From this point of view, one might say that mixed feelings are not proof that there is no love. Rather, they are a sign that the relationship is deep and touches the whole of you. The contradiction doesn't have to be resolved; it can be accepted as part of a living, complicated love.
ambivalence.practice: Write one sentence that holds both love and irritation, with no "but": "I love you, and it's very hard for me with you."

quote.text: Man is broad, even too broad; I would narrow him down.
quote.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
quote.source: The Brothers Karamazov (1880), words of Dmitri Karamazov

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, a departure, or even the death of a loved one who had been ill for a long time is often hidden deep inside. Nikolai Berdyaev wrote that the "ethics of law" is ready to condemn any feeling that doesn't fit the general rule: "you mustn't feel that way." Lev Shestov rebelled all his life against "general truths" that cannot hear the concrete, suffering person. From their point of view, one might say that relief is a living feeling of a living person who carried a weight for a long time. Moralizing demands that you feel nothing but sorrow, but a real soul is more complex than rules. Berdyaev believed a person's freedom includes the right to be honest with oneself, even when one's feelings don't match what is expected. Relief and love can exist at the same time. Neither cancels the other, and neither makes you a worse person.
guilty_relief.practice: Write yourself the sentence you wouldn't dare say out loud: "I feel lighter." Next to it: "And that doesn't cancel my love."

indifference.text: Sometimes where something "ought" to move you, it's quiet inside, and that feels unsettling. Nikolai Berdyaev criticized the "ethics of law," which prescribes not only actions but feelings: here you're supposed to grieve, here to feel compassion. He believed a genuine feeling cannot be summoned on command: it is born of freedom, not of obligation. From this point of view, one might say indifference is not always coldness. Sometimes it's tiredness, sometimes protection from something too strong, sometimes simply a pause after which the feeling will come by itself. Lev Shestov would add that a living person is not obliged to conform to general norms even in what they feel. You can admit, "Right now I don't feel what's expected of me," and not judge yourself for it.
indifference.practice: Honestly name what you feel right now instead of what you "should," even if it's "nothing" or "tiredness." Write it down without judging.

escape.text: The urge to drop everything, the job, the city, the role, can be very strong. All his life Nikolai Berdyaev kept leaving circles where he felt confined: the gentry milieu, Marxism, many philosophical and church groups. In Self-Knowledge he wrote that he never felt fully "one of them" in any milieu. His main theme is freedom, and the main threat to freedom is slavery to society, the state, the family, a role. From his point of view, one might say the urge to escape is the voice of a freedom that feels caged. But Berdyaev distinguished "freedom from," the wish to break out, and "freedom for," the wish to create something new. The first without the second only swaps one cage for another. You can ask yourself not only what you are running from, but also what you want to create.
escape.practice: Finish two sentences: "I want to be free from…" and "I want freedom so that I can…" Compare which of them sounds stronger.

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone who is unavailable or "not right" can be strong and tormenting. Nikolai Berdyaev wrote a great deal about eros, in his early essay "The Metaphysics of Sex and Love" and in The Meaning of the Creative Act. For him love is not just a feeling or a social contract but a mysterious creative force that often doesn't coincide with accepted frameworks. Following Plato, Berdyaev saw in eros a longing for wholeness, a striving for a fullness that a person lacks. From his point of view, one might say a forbidden attraction speaks not only of a particular person but of your deep thirst for fullness, aliveness, recognition. Berdyaev gave no recipes and passed no quick verdicts. But he invited us to look closely at desire: what is it really calling the soul toward?
forbidden_attraction.practice: Without naming anyone, write: "This attraction says that what I'm missing is…" What quality of life stands behind it?

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and their judgment can squeeze you from the inside. Nikolai Berdyaev wrote about "objectification": in society a person turns into an object, someone's assessment, a label, a role. Under others' gaze we feel like a thing being examined and rated. From his point of view, one might say social anxiety is the fear of being objectified, reduced to what people will think of us. But Berdyaev insisted that a person is never reducible to an object. A person is a mystery no assessment can exhaust. He distinguished communion, a living meeting of two persons, from impersonal "society," where everyone rates everyone. Anxiety belongs to the second. Sometimes it helps to look among people not for an audience but for at least one conversation partner with whom a real meeting is possible.
social_anxiety.practice: At your next gathering, find one person with your eyes whom you could really talk to, and address yourself to them first.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is hard: the future is unknown and you can't lean on it. Lev Shestov rebelled all his life against the rule of "necessity," the notion that everything is already predetermined by laws and general truths. For him uncertainty was not only a threat but also an openness: where nothing is predetermined, there is room for the unexpected, for what no logic would have predicted. Berdyaev, too, saw the future not as a finished script but as a space of freedom where a person takes part in creating something new. From their point of view, one might say uncertainty is the other side of freedom. Being afraid of it is understandable. But not knowing the future also means it isn't closed yet. You can allow yourself not to know, and still notice that you are able to influence it.
uncertainty.practice: Write: "I don't know what will happen. But precisely because of that, it's still possible that…" Add one thing that would be truly precious to you.

waiting.text: Waiting, for an answer, for results, for news, can be agonizing. Lev Shestov wrote a great deal about the biblical Job, who lost everything and waited for an answer: not consolation from his friends but a real answer to his cry. Shestov valued Job for refusing ready-made explanations and continuing to demand a living answer. Berdyaev, for his part, said that waiting for the future should not be passive: a person doesn't only wait but also takes part and creates. From their point of view, one might say waiting is a legitimate state in which you don't need to pretend to be calm. Like Job, you can honestly admit your impatience. And, as Berdyaev advised, you can refuse to hand your whole life over to waiting: while you wait, you are still able to create in the present.
waiting.practice: Admit your impatience in one sentence: "Waiting is hard for me." Then choose one small creative task for the next hour.

regret.text: Regret over what you did or didn't do can come back again and again. In Athens and Jerusalem, Lev Shestov boldly rebelled against the idea that the past is final and irrevocable, against what he called the power of necessity over human beings. He examined the medieval thinkers' dispute over whether God can make what has been not to have been, and he sided with the living person for whom the past's final verdict is unbearable. Berdyaev came at it from another side: in the "ethics of creativity" a person answers mistakes not only with repentance but by creating something new. From their point of view, one might say the past does not have the last word on who you will become. Regret is legitimate. But it can become not a verdict but the start of a new response.
regret.practice: Write down what you regret, and then: "My new response to this could be…" One small creative action.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is the ache for someone no one else can replace. Nikolai Berdyaev built his philosophy on the idea of the person: unique, unrepeatable, not reducible to anything general. For him every human being is a whole world, and no general category exhausts them. From this point of view, longing for a particular person is a recognition of their uniqueness: what you miss is not "somebody" but precisely them. Berdyaev also wrote a lot about longing itself: in Self-Knowledge he confessed that this feeling accompanied him all his life, and he saw in it a sign that the soul reaches for something greater than the everyday. Longing does not cancel love; it bears witness to it. You can live through it as faithfulness to the unrepeatable meeting you had.
longing.practice: Write down three traits of this person that belong only to them. Let yourself simply remember them.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world, from grim news, war, injustice, can be enormous. Berdyaev and Shestov, who lived through war, revolution and exile, knew this feeling. Berdyaev often recalled Ivan Karamazov's question in Dostoevsky: can one accept a world harmony built on the suffering of even one child? Berdyaev believed the suffering of a single person cannot be justified by any general goal. Shestov rebelled against every explanation that makes another's pain "necessary." From their point of view, one might say your pain for the world is faithfulness to the value of every human being. You don't need to be ashamed of it or to muffle it. But you can give it a direction: into compassion, help, a creative response, without letting it destroy you.
world_pain.practice: Choose one concrete, small way to respond to what hurts: helping, writing a letter, donating. Do it, and let yourself stop there.

rejection.text: Rejection hurts: you weren't accepted, weren't chosen, weren't wanted. Lev Shestov wrote for decades understood by few; many found his thought strange, awkward and too sharp. He took the side of those rejected by "general truths," the criteria by which the world decides who is needed and who isn't. His favorite figure was Job, who refused to accept the verdict of the friends explaining his misfortunes. Berdyaev added that a person is defined neither by public recognition nor by anyone else's judgment: a person is deeper and freer than any label. From their point of view, one might say rejection is someone's assessment, not the final truth about you. The pain of it is real. But it doesn't have to become your own verdict on yourself.
rejection.practice: Write: "I was rejected, but I don't agree that…" Finish it with what you refuse to accept in the other person's judgment.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned is a deep fear of being left alone. In Solitude and Society (I and the World of Objects), Nikolai Berdyaev wrote about solitude as an inseparable part of a person's existence: precisely because each person is unique, in some way they are always alone. But Berdyaev didn't stop there. He distinguished a loneliness that no outward company can overcome from genuine communion, the meeting of two persons, "I" and "Thou." Such communion doesn't guarantee that someone will stay forever, but it makes the bond alive. From his point of view, one might say the fear of abandonment is a sign of a deep need for communion. That need can't be satisfied by controlling the other person. But it can be nourished, through meetings in which you are seen as a person.
abandonment.practice: Recall a recent moment when you felt truly heard. Write it down: it's proof that such meetings are possible.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love wounds deeply. Nikolai Berdyaev considered love one of the highest forms of freedom: it can't be earned, forced or bought. Love, for Berdyaev, is a creative act that sees in another an unrepeatable person. But this freedom also holds pain: the other is free too, and may not respond. From his point of view, one might say unrequited love was not a mistake. You saw the other's unrepeatable face, and that seeing was a genuine creative act. Berdyaev never promised that love would be mutual. But he believed the creative act of love itself is not lost: it changes the one who loves and stays in them. Your capacity to love so deeply is not a weakness but evidence of your freedom.
unrequited.practice: Write down what this love opened up in you: what feelings, what strength, what tenderness you discovered in yourself.

humiliation.text: Humiliation wounds deeply, as if your dignity had been taken away. One of Dostoevsky's novels is called Humiliated and Insulted, and Berdyaev and Shestov both wrote a lot about how he portrayed such people. In Notes from Underground the humiliated hero grows bitter, and his hurt turns into malice. Shestov saw in the "underground man" the truth of a protest against a world that crushes the living person. In Dostoevsky: An Interpretation, Berdyaev stressed that every human being, even a humiliated one, has the dignity of a person that no one can take away. From their point of view, one might say humiliation is a wound that can't be denied. But it speaks of violence done to you, not of your worth. You can acknowledge the pain and refuse to accept the other's view of you.
humiliation.practice: Write: "I was humiliated, but there remains in me…" Name one thing no one can take from you.

body_shame.text: Being unhappy with your body can be a heavy background to life. Nikolai Berdyaev argued with the tradition that separates soul from body and treats the body as something lower. For him the person is a wholeness: spirit, soul and body together. He stressed that the body is not just a shell but part of the image of the person, its expression in the world; the human face seemed especially expressive to him. From his point of view, one might say body shame is often born of "objectification": we look at ourselves as an object to be rated and compared with a norm. But a person is not reducible to an object. Your body is not an exhibit to be graded but part of your uniqueness, of how you are present in the world. It doesn't have to meet a standard to be yours.
body_shame.practice: Look at your face in the mirror for one minute, not as an assessor but as someone greeting a person they know. What do you see?

illness.text: Illness, when your body lets you down, can take away your strength, your plans, your familiar sense of yourself. Lev Shestov wrote a great deal about the biblical Job, who lost everything, his health included, and was covered in sores. His friends came to comfort him and began explaining why it had happened, as if the misfortune followed a rule. Job refused to accept their explanations. Shestov saw a great truth in this: a suffering person is not obliged to agree that their pain is "right" or "deserved." From his point of view, one might say you don't need to look for meaning or blame in your illness. You can speak honestly about your pain and protest against it. Berdyaev would add that a person is more than their body and their illness: they keep their freedom, at least in how they meet what is happening.
illness.practice: If someone explains your illness to you, you can answer silently: "I don't need an explanation. I need to be heard."

pride.text: Pride in what you've done is a healthy feeling, and you can enjoy it. In The Meaning of the Creative Act, subtitled An Essay in the Justification of Man, Nikolai Berdyaev argued that human beings are called to create, to continue the creation of the world by making what was not there before. For him creativity wasn't limited to art: a job well done, a solution found, a garden grown are creative acts too. At the same time, Berdyaev distinguished creative dignity from vainglory: vainglory closes in on itself and compares itself with others, while creative joy is directed at what has been made and at the world. From his point of view, one might say healthy pride is the joy of having taken part in creation. You added something to the world. You can enjoy that calmly, without apologizing and without comparing.
pride.practice: Look at what you've made and tell yourself: "This didn't exist, and now it does." Stay with that feeling for a minute.

melancholy.text: Bright sadness is a quiet feeling in which sorrow and tenderness are intertwined. In Self-Knowledge, Nikolai Berdyaev distinguished longing, fear and boredom. Boredom, he observed, pulls downward, toward emptiness, while longing, on the contrary, is turned upward: it is a yearning for something higher, for something greater than the everyday. He confessed that longing accompanied him all his life, and he saw in it a sign of the soul's depth, not an illness. From his point of view, one might say melancholy is not a defeat but a sensitivity to the fact that the world is not exhausted by everyday life. This sadness says that there lives in you a striving toward something greater: beauty, meaning, the eternal. It doesn't need to be treated or chased away. You can live bright sadness as a quiet reminder of your depth.
melancholy.practice: Ask yourself: "What, beyond my everyday life, is my soul longing for right now?" Write down the first thing that comes.
